transcript:
Section 1: Library Orientation: A Student and the Facilities Manager

M: Good morning, welcome to the Westbridge University Library. I'm Daniel, the facilities manager. You must be the new PhD student, right?
W: Yes, that's me. I'm Lin, from the Department of Environmental Science. I received an email about a library orientation session, but I'm afraid I got a bit lost.
M: No problem at all. Let me give you a quick tour and explain how everything works. First, your student card is also your library card. You'll need it to enter the building after 8 p.m. and to borrow any materials.
W: Oh, I see. So I can't just walk in with my bag?
M: Exactly. The main entrance is open from 7 a.m. to 10 p.m. on weekdays, but on weekends it closes at 8 p.m. However, the 24-hour study room on the ground floor is always accessible with your card.
W: That's good to know. And how many books can I borrow at once?
M: For PhD students, the limit is 20 items, and the standard loan period is 4 weeks. You can renew online up to three times, unless someone else has reserved the item.
W: Right. And what about journals? Can I take those out?
M: No, journals are for reference only. You can read them in the reading room, but they can't be borrowed. However, you can photocopy articles for personal use, as long as you follow copyright regulations.
W: I see. Is there a charge for photocopying?
M: Yes, it's 5 pence per page for black and white, and 20 pence for colour. You'll need to buy a copy card from the machine near the printers.
W: OK. Now, I'm particularly interested in environmental science materials. Where are they located?
M: The science collection is on the second floor, but the environmental science section is actually on the third floor, in the north wing. You'll find both books and recent journals there.
W: Great. And do you have any quiet study areas?
M: Yes, the silent study zone is on the fourth floor. It's strictly for individual study, so no group discussions are allowed. If you need to work in a group, you can book a group study room on the first floor. Those rooms can be reserved online up to two weeks in advance.
W: That sounds useful. One more thing: I heard there's a workshop on referencing next week. Is that open to all students?
M: Yes, it's open to all postgraduate students. It's on Wednesday at 2 p.m. in the seminar room on the ground floor. You don't need to book, just turn up.
W: Perfect. Thanks for your help.
M: You're welcome. If you have any other questions, just ask at the help desk.

Section 2: Simulated Listening: Campus Library Orientation

Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Northside Campus Library. Thank you for coming along today; I know you have a lot to take in during your first week, so I’ll keep this brief and practical. My name is Sarah, and I’m the library services coordinator here. I’ll give you some practical information about using the library this term, covering opening hours, borrowing, study spaces, printing and copying, and our workshops. Please hold questions until the end, and I’ll do my best to answer them all then.

First, opening hours. From Monday to Friday, we open at 8 a.m. and close at 10 p.m. On Saturdays, we open at 9 a.m. and close at 6 p.m. On Sundays, we are closed. During exam weeks, we stay open until midnight from Monday to Thursday, but the weekend hours remain the same. These extended hours are designed to give you more time for revision, so do check the notices near the entrance for the exact dates.

Now, borrowing. Undergraduate students can borrow up to 12 books at a time for three weeks. Postgraduate students can borrow up to 20 books for four weeks. You can renew books online twice, unless someone else has reserved them. If you return a book late, you pay a fine of 50 cents per day per book. The maximum fine is 20 dollars. We send reminder emails before items are due, so please keep an eye on your student inbox.

Next, study spaces. The ground floor is for group study. You can talk there, but please keep your voice down. The first floor is a quiet zone for individual study. The second floor has computer workstations and a media room. You need to book the media room at the front desk at least one day in advance. Please remember that the quiet zone is strictly for silent work, and staff may ask you to move if conversations disturb others.

About printing and copying. There are printers on the first and second floors. Printing costs 10 cents per page for black and white, and 30 cents for colour. You can add credit to your student card at the machine near the entrance. If you run into any problems with the machines, a member of staff at the front desk will be happy to help.

Finally, workshops. This month, we offer a workshop on referencing and citation on the 15th at 2 p.m. in Room 204. Another workshop on using databases will be on the 22nd at 3 p.m. in Room 101. You can sign up on our website or at the front desk. Spaces are limited, so please register early to avoid disappointment.

That’s all from me. Now, are there any questions?

Section 3: Academic Listening: The Campus Sustainability Audit

TUTOR: Good morning, everyone. Thanks for coming to this extra session on the campus sustainability audit. As you know, your group has been collecting data on energy use in the library and the student union building. Let's review what you've found so far. Maria, could you start with the library? MARIA: Yes, sure. We monitored electricity consumption for four weeks. The library used about 12,000 kilowatt-hours per week on average. That's higher than we expected. But then we realised the old lighting system was the main problem. TUTOR: Right. And did you look at the heating? MARIA: We did, but the data was incomplete because the sensors were faulty. So we couldn't draw conclusions about heating. TUTOR: That's fine. It's important to acknowledge limitations. Now, Tom, what about the student union? TOM: Well, the union building was renovated last year, so it has new windows and insulation. As a result, its energy use is much lower—around 7,500 kilowatt-hours per week. But we noticed that the cafe area still uses old refrigerators, which consume a lot of power. TUTOR: Good observation. So what recommendations are you planning to make? MARIA: For the library, we suggest replacing all the lights with LED bulbs. We estimate that would cut electricity use by about 30 percent. TUTOR: That sounds reasonable. And for the union? TOM: We recommend replacing the old refrigerators with energy-efficient models. Also, we think the university should install solar panels on the union roof, because it gets a lot of sunlight. TUTOR: Solar panels are a bigger investment, but they could be a long-term solution. Have you considered the cost? TOM: Not yet, but we plan to research that next week. TUTOR: Good. Now, before you write your report, remember to structure it clearly. Start with an introduction that states the purpose of the audit. Then present your methodology—how you collected data. After that, give your findings, and finally your recommendations. Also, make sure you cite any sources you use. MARIA: Should we include graphs? TUTOR: Yes, graphs are helpful, but label them clearly. And keep the report concise—around 2,000 words is fine. TOM: What about the deadline? TUTOR: The report is due on the 15th of next month. Submit it online via the portal. MARIA: Okay. And will we get feedback before the final submission? TUTOR: Yes, you'll receive written feedback within a week of submitting a draft. I suggest you send me a draft by the 8th. TOM: That's helpful. One more thing—can we interview the building managers? TUTOR: Absolutely. In fact, I can arrange that for you. Just email me the questions you want to ask. MARIA: Great. We'll do that. TUTOR: Alright, then. Keep up the good work. See you next week.

Section 4: The Hidden Cost of Fast Fashion: A Lecture on Clothing Lifespans

Good morning, everyone. Today I want to talk about something that affects all of us: the clothes we wear and how long we keep them. In particular, I'll be discussing the environmental impact of what's often called 'fast fashion' – a business model where inexpensive clothing is produced rapidly in response to new trends. My focus will be on the hidden costs of this model, especially the resources used and the waste generated.

First, let's consider how clothing consumption has changed. In the past, people typically owned fewer garments and kept them for years, often repairing them. But over the last two decades, the average number of times a garment is worn before being discarded has fallen dramatically. For example, in some high-income countries, the average number of wears per garment has dropped by around 36 percent compared to fifteen years ago. This means that even though clothes are cheaper, we are buying more and using them less.

So, what happens to all these clothes? A significant proportion ends up in landfill or is incinerated. Globally, it's estimated that the equivalent of one garbage truck full of textiles is burned or sent to landfill every second. That's a staggering figure. And when clothes decompose in landfill, they release methane, a potent greenhouse gas. Synthetic fabrics, like polyester, do not decompose easily and can persist for hundreds of years.

Now, you might think that donating clothes is a solution. While donation is better than throwing clothes away, it's not a complete answer. Many donated clothes are exported to developing countries, where they can overwhelm local markets and disrupt local textile industries. Moreover, only a small fraction of donated clothes are actually resold in the receiving country; much of it is of low quality and eventually becomes waste there.

Another issue is the production phase. Growing cotton requires large amounts of water and pesticides. It's been calculated that producing one kilogram of cotton – roughly enough for one T-shirt and a pair of jeans – can require up to 20,000 litres of water. That's equivalent to what one person might drink over several years. Synthetic fibres, on the other hand, are made from petroleum, a non-renewable resource, and their production is energy-intensive.

So, what can be done? There are several strategies. First, we can extend the active life of garments by designing them to be more durable and repairable. Second, consumers can shift towards buying second-hand or renting clothes. Third, governments can implement policies such as extended producer responsibility, which makes manufacturers responsible for the waste their products create. Finally, raising consumer awareness is crucial; many people are simply unaware of the hidden costs.

To sum up, fast fashion offers cheap and trendy clothes, but at a significant environmental and social cost. By understanding these hidden costs, we can make more informed choices as consumers and support policies that encourage a more sustainable clothing industry. Thank you for listening.

grammar.title: 学术句子的主干、修饰关系与名词短语；被动表达
grammar.explanation: 学术英语句子通常有明确的主干（主语+谓语+宾语），修饰成分（如定语从句、介词短语）用来补充信息。名词短语可能包含多个修饰语。被动语态常用于客观描述，强调动作的承受者。例如：'The main entrance is open from 7 a.m. to 10 p.m.' 主干是 'The main entrance is open'，介词短语作时间状语。'Journals are for reference only' 是系表结构。'Those rooms can be reserved online' 是被动语态，强调房间被预订。
grammar.example: Those rooms can be reserved online up to two weeks in advance.
